title: Senior's toolkit: functions and the call stack
summary: The Call Stack window, stepping in and out, navigating to definitions, extracting methods and asserting assumptions.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: functions and the call stack
steps.body: Once code is split into functions, the question is always "who called this, with what?". These are the tools that answer it, and the shortcuts that make splitting code cheap.

toolkit.what: Shows every function that is running right now, newest at the top. Double-click a frame to see that function's variables at the moment it made the call.
flags: Debug > Windows > Call Stack, or Ctrl+Alt+C
the CALL STACK section of the Run and Debug view
jump to it and see its own Locals
toolkit.example: Stop in Factorial(1): the stack shows Factorial(1), Factorial(2), Factorial(3), Main
toolkit.when: a function gets a bad argument and you need to know who passed it

toolkit.what: Step into a call to follow it, step out when you have seen enough, step over calls you trust.
flags: step into the function called on this line
run to the end of this function and stop in the caller
run the whole line, calls included
toolkit.example: F11 into Area(...), check the arguments, Shift+F11 back out

toolkit.what: Navigate code without searching: go to where a function is defined, or list every place that calls it before you change it.
flags: go back to where you were (Visual Studio; Alt+Left in VS Code)
toolkit.example: Cursor on CalculateDamage, Shift+F12: 4 callers to check before changing its parameters

toolkit.what: Select some lines and turn them into a new function. The IDE works out the parameters and the return value, so it cannot change behaviour by mistake.
flags: Ctrl+R, Ctrl+M, or Ctrl+. > Extract method
type the new name straight away; every use updates
toolkit.example: Select the 6 lines that compute the score, Ctrl+R, Ctrl+M, name it ScoreFor

toolkit.what: State an assumption in code. In a Debug build the debugger stops (or the program fails) when it is false; Release builds remove the check.
flags: what must be true here, e.g. `n >= 0`
what went wrong, shown when it fails

steps.prompt: Your recursive maze solver crashes. The terminal shows this. What is the most likely cause?
options: `Walk` calls itself without ever reaching its base case, for example it revisits cells it has already been to
The program ran out of disk space
steps.explain: "Repeated N times" with the same frame means one function called itself over and over. Check the base case, and check that every call moves toward it (mark visited cells). `<<Main>$>g__Walk` is how a local function named `Walk` appears in a stack trace.

steps.prompt: Match each key to what it does.
pairs: finish this function and return to the caller
go to where the function is defined
extract the selected lines into a method

steps.prompt: The print comes *after* the recursive call. What does this print?
steps.explain: Each call waits for the one below it. `Count(0)` returns first, then `Count(1)` prints 1, then 2, then 3. In the Call Stack window you would see four `Count` frames at the deepest point.

steps.prompt: `Area` gets a negative width from somewhere. Put the debugging steps in order.
lines: Put a conditional breakpoint in Area: width < 0
Press F5 and wait for it to stop
Open the Call Stack and double-click the caller's frame
Read the caller's Locals to see where the negative width came from
Fix the caller and add Debug.Assert(width >= 0) in Area

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When a function gets a bad value, the bug is usually in the caller: open the Call Stack before you change the function. Press Shift+F12 before changing any signature, and use Extract method instead of copying lines by hand.
